questions.stem: A client presents with fever, severe headache, photophobia, and nuchal rigidity, and a family member reports the client was well yesterday. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Meningitis requiring urgent evaluation because fever, severe headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness suggest meningeal inflammation.","B":"Subarachnoid hemorrhage requiring urgent neuroimaging because severe headache and photophobia can accompany meningeal irritation after bleeding.","C":"Migraine with aura requiring symptomatic therapy because severe headache and photophobia can occur without an intracranial infection.","D":"Viral respiratory illness with tension headache because fever and headache can coexist during an otherwise uncomplicated infection."}}
questions.rationale: CDC identifies fever, headache, and stiff neck as common meningitis symptoms, often accompanied by photophobia, nausea, vomiting, or altered mental status, and advises prompt medical evaluation because bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency. Subarachnoid hemorrhage can cause meningeal irritation but does not by itself explain this infectious symptom cluster; migraine can cause severe headache and photophobia but not the characteristic fever with nuchal rigidity; an uncomplicated respiratory illness does not adequately explain marked meningeal signs.
questions.source_detail: CDC lists fever, headache, and stiff neck as common meningitis symptoms, often with photophobia, and states that bacterial meningitis requires urgent treatment.

questions.stem: A teenage client presents with sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Which action is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Obtain Doppler ultrasonography before urgent consultation, because imaging should always be completed before surgical evaluation of acute scrotal pain.","B":"Arrange immediate urologic evaluation for possible testicular torsion, because prompt detorsion is critical and treatment is ideally within 4–6 hours.","C":"Treat presumptive epididymitis with antibiotics and outpatient follow-up, because acute unilateral scrotal pain in adolescents is usually infectious.","D":"Attempt manual detorsion and discharge if the pain resolves, because successful bedside detorsion eliminates the need for surgical exploration."}}
questions.rationale: The EAU Paediatric Urology guideline identifies testicular torsion as a urologic emergency requiring immediate treatment. Salvage depends strongly on time to detorsion and the degree of twisting, with surgery ideally performed within 4–6 hours after symptom onset. Doppler ultrasonography can assist evaluation but should not delay intervention when torsion is suspected. Manual detorsion may be attempted while awaiting surgery but does not replace operative exploration and fixation. Empiric outpatient treatment for epididymitis would create an unsafe delay in this presentation.
questions.source_name: European Association of Urology — Paediatric Urology Guideline: Acute Scrotum
questions.source_detail: EAU states that testicular torsion requires immediate treatment, that earlier detorsion improves salvage, ideally within 4–6 hours, and that Doppler imaging or manual detorsion must not delay surgery.

questions.stem: A client with benign prostatic hyperplasia has severe lower abdominal discomfort, has been unable to void for several hours, and has a palpable distended bladder. Which condition and response are most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Acute cystitis requiring urine culture and antibiotics first, because infection commonly causes a full palpable bladder with complete inability to void.","B":"Renal colic requiring analgesia and imaging first, because ureteral obstruction commonly causes a palpable distended bladder and inability to void.","C":"Acute urinary retention requiring prompt bladder decompression, usually with catheter drainage, while the cause of obstruction is evaluated promptly.","D":"Chronic urinary retention requiring routine outpatient follow-up, because urgent bladder drainage is unnecessary without infection or kidney injury."}}
questions.rationale: NIDDK describes acute urinary retention as a sudden inability to urinate despite a full bladder; lower abdominal pain and swelling are typical, and BPH increases risk by obstructing urine flow. Acute retention requires immediate bladder drainage with a catheter to relieve pain and reduce risk of bladder or kidney injury while the cause is addressed. Cystitis or renal colic does not best explain a painfully distended bladder with complete inability to void, and this acute symptomatic presentation should not be managed as routine chronic retention.
questions.source_name: NIDDK — Urinary Retention: Definition, Symptoms, and Treatment
questions.source_detail: NIDDK states that acute urinary retention causes sudden inability to urinate with a full bladder, BPH is a risk factor, and acute retention is treated by immediate catheter drainage.

questions.stem: A client develops a severe systemic allergic-like reaction immediately after iodinated IV contrast. An IgE-mediated mechanism has not been established. Which principle should guide emergency treatment?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use observation alone initially, because non-IgE contrast reactions cannot produce the airway or circulatory findings seen in severe allergic reactions.","B":"Treat only cutaneous symptoms, because allergic-like contrast reactions remain limited to skin findings when prior sensitization has not occurred.","C":"Delay emergency treatment until the mechanism is confirmed, because epinephrine is appropriate only after an IgE-mediated allergy is established.","D":"Treat the severe allergic-like reaction using the same emergency approach as an equivalent allergic reaction, including epinephrine when indicated."}}
questions.rationale: The ACR Manual distinguishes allergic-like contrast reactions from physiologic reactions because allergic-like reactions can clinically resemble true allergic reactions even when an antigen-antibody mechanism is not established. A severe allergic-like reaction can involve airway compromise, bronchospasm, hypotension, or anaphylactic shock and should be treated according to the corresponding acute allergic-reaction protocol, including epinephrine when indicated. Waiting for mechanistic confirmation, limiting treatment to skin symptoms, or observation alone would be unsafe in a severe systemic reaction.
questions.source_name: American College of Radiology — Manual on Contrast Media
questions.source_detail: ACR classifies acute contrast reactions as allergic-like or physiologic and provides emergency treatment tables for severe allergic-like reactions, including epinephrine when indicated.

questions.stem: A nurse is interpreting the baseline fetal heart rate during labor. Which baseline range is considered normal under the standard three-tier intrapartum interpretation system?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A baseline of 90–110 beats/min, because this range represents the standard normal fetal baseline during labor when variability remains moderate.","B":"A baseline of 100–170 beats/min, because values throughout this wider range are categorized as normal regardless of the rest of the tracing.","C":"A baseline of 120–180 beats/min, because fetal tachycardia is not defined until the baseline remains above 180 beats/min during labor.","D":"A baseline of 110–160 beats/min, because this is the standard normal fetal heart-rate baseline range used for intrapartum interpretation."}}
questions.rationale: The standardized NICHD/ACOG three-tier terminology defines a normal fetal heart-rate baseline as 110–160 beats/min. A baseline below 110 is bradycardia and above 160 is tachycardia when present for the required baseline interval; overall tracing interpretation also considers variability, accelerations, and decelerations. The alternative ranges therefore do not match the standard baseline definition.
questions.source_name: ACOG — Fetal Heart Tracing: Standardized Intrapartum Interpretation
questions.source_detail: ACOG describes the normal fetal heart-rate baseline as 110–160 beats/min and uses this range in Category I tracing interpretation.
